title: Decorators
summary: **Decorators** are functions prefixed with `@` that attach reusable behavior or metadata to classes, methods, accessors, properties, and parameters — the foundation of frameworks like Angular and NestJS, enabled via `experimentalDecorators` (legacy) or the newer TC39 standard.

subtopics.title: What decorators are
subtopics.explanation: A decorator is a function applied with @ syntax to a declaration. The compiler calls it with information about the thing it decorates, letting the decorator observe, modify, or replace it. Decorators are a declarative way to attach cross-cutting behavior (logging, validation, dependency injection) without cluttering the decorated code.

subtopics.title: Class decorators
subtopics.explanation: A class decorator receives the class constructor and can inspect it, replace it, or attach metadata. Frameworks use class decorators like @Component or @Injectable to register a class and configure it. Returning a new constructor lets a decorator extend or wrap the class.

subtopics.title: Method and accessor decorators
subtopics.explanation: A method decorator receives the target, the method name, and (in legacy mode) the property descriptor, so it can wrap or replace the method — e.g. to add logging, timing, or memoization. Accessor decorators work the same way for getters/setters.

subtopics.title: Property and parameter decorators
subtopics.explanation: Property decorators run on a field declaration and are typically used to record metadata (e.g. validation rules) rather than alter behavior directly. Parameter decorators receive the position of a constructor or method parameter and are central to dependency injection, marking which dependency to inject.

subtopics.title: Metadata and reflect-metadata
subtopics.explanation: Decorators often store metadata about a declaration for a framework to read later. With emitDecoratorMetadata and the reflect-metadata polyfill, TypeScript emits design-time type info (like a parameter's type) that DI containers read to resolve dependencies automatically.
subtopics.example:
import 'reflect-metadata';
// @Injectable() reads constructor param types via Reflect.getMetadata('design:paramtypes', target)

subtopics.title: Common uses: Angular and NestJS
subtopics.explanation: Angular uses @Component, @Injectable, @Input, and @Output to declare components, services, and bindings. NestJS uses @Controller, @Get, @Injectable, and @Body to define routes and inject dependencies. Decorators turn plain classes into framework-recognized building blocks declaratively.

subtopics.title: Enabling decorators and the TC39 standard
subtopics.explanation: Legacy (experimental) decorators require experimentalDecorators in tsconfig and use the (target, key, descriptor) signature; emitDecoratorMetadata adds type metadata. The newer TC39 Stage-3 decorators (supported from TypeScript 5.0) use a different (value, context) signature, are enabled by default, and do not emit design metadata — frameworks are migrating gradually.

foundations.overview: Decorators are a syntax for attaching behavior and metadata to declarations using @ functions. There are two flavors: the long-standing legacy/experimental decorators (gated by the experimentalDecorators flag, with optional emitDecoratorMetadata) that frameworks like Angular and NestJS rely on, and the newer TC39 Stage-3 standard decorators (TypeScript 5.0+) which use a different signature and are on by default. Decorators let frameworks turn plain classes into recognized components, controllers, and injectables declaratively.
foundations.formalDefinition: A decorator is a function evaluated at class-definition time and applied to a class, method, accessor, property, or parameter. The compiler invokes it with details of the target; the decorator may observe it, attach metadata, or (for class/method/accessor decorators) replace it.
foundations.whyItMatters: Decorators power the most popular TypeScript backend/frontend frameworks — Angular and NestJS are built around them — and they appear in DI, ORMs (TypeORM), and validation libraries (class-validator). Interviewers use them to test understanding of metaprogramming, the experimental-vs-standard split, and the metadata mechanism behind DI.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a decorator as a function that runs once when the class is defined, handed the thing it decorates, with the chance to register, wrap, or annotate it before any instances exist.
foundations.browserPerspective: Legacy decorators are erased into helper calls (__decorate) the browser runs at definition time; metadata requires the reflect-metadata polyfill loaded in the bundle. Standard TC39 decorators compile to spec-defined runtime calls. Either way, the @ syntax itself is transformed away — the browser runs ordinary JavaScript.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Angular component/service declaration (@Component, @Injectable), NestJS controllers and DI (@Controller, @Get, @Injectable), TypeORM entity mapping (@Entity, @Column), and validation (@IsEmail) in class-validator.
foundations.businessImpact: Declarative decorators keep framework wiring concise and consistent, speeding feature delivery and reducing boilerplate-related bugs that delay releases.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Decorators centralize cross-cutting concerns (logging, auth, validation, DI) so business logic stays clean, but they add a layer of indirection and a compiler-flag/runtime dependency the whole team must understand.
foundations.performanceImpact: Decorators run once at class-definition time, so runtime cost is generally minimal. emitDecoratorMetadata and reflect-metadata add bundle size and a small startup cost; method-wrapping decorators add overhead per call proportional to what they do.
commonUseCases: Dependency injection via parameter decorators and metadata
Cross-cutting method wrappers (logging, caching, timing, auth guards)

commonMisconceptions.myth: Decorators run every time a decorated method is called.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A decorator function runs once, at class-definition time. It may install a wrapper that runs per call, but the decorator itself is evaluated only once.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Legacy and TC39 decorators are interchangeable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They have different signatures and semantics. Legacy uses (target, key, descriptor) and supports emitDecoratorMetadata; TC39 Stage-3 uses (value, context) and emits no design metadata, so framework code is not directly portable between them.

visualExplorer.caption: Step through @log on a method and watch the decorator replace it with a wrapper at definition time.

config.intro: Trace a legacy @log method decorator applied to greet() to add a console line on each call.

steps.name: Define the class
steps.detail: At class-definition time the compiler reaches the @log-decorated greet method.

steps.name: Invoke the decorator
steps.detail: log(target, 'greet', descriptor) runs once, receiving the method's property descriptor.

steps.name: Capture the original
steps.detail: The decorator saves descriptor.value (the original greet) so it can still be called.

steps.name: Install a wrapper
steps.detail: It sets descriptor.value to a new function that logs, then delegates to the original via apply.

steps.name: Call at runtime
steps.detail: Every later greet() call runs the wrapper: it logs and then returns the original method's result.

codeLab.title: Build a memoize method-wrapper
codeLab.instructions: A method decorator caches results by argument. Decorators need experimentalDecorators, so implement the wrapper logic as a function makeMemoized(fn) that returns a memoized version (the same logic a @memoize decorator would install). Repeated calls with the same arg should reuse the cached result.
hints: Keep a Map from argument to result.
On each call, return the cached value if present; otherwise compute, store, and return it.

debuggingLab.title: Decorators not enabled / metadata missing
debuggingLab.symptom: Using @Injectable triggers 'Experimental support for decorators is a feature that is subject to change' or DI fails because constructor param types are undefined.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Legacy decorators require experimentalDecorators in tsconfig to compile, and DI that resolves by type needs emitDecoratorMetadata plus the reflect-metadata polyfill so the compiler emits and the runtime can read design:paramtypes. Missing any of these means the container can't see the constructor's types.
commonMistakes: Not importing 'reflect-metadata' once at the app entry point.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Enable the compiler flags and load the metadata polyfill so type-based DI works.

theory.question: What are decorators in TypeScript and what can they decorate?
theory.directAnswer: Decorators are functions applied with @ syntax that the compiler invokes at class-definition time to observe, modify, attach metadata to, or replace a declaration. You can decorate classes, methods, accessors, properties, and parameters. They are the basis of declarative frameworks like Angular and NestJS, where annotations like @Component or @Injectable register and configure classes.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Special functions attached to declarations via @ that run when the class is defined.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To express cross-cutting concerns and framework wiring declaratively without polluting the decorated code.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler calls the decorator with target details; class/method/accessor decorators may return a replacement, while property/parameter decorators usually record metadata.

theory.whyImportant: Decorators underpin the dominant TypeScript frameworks and ORMs, so understanding them is essential for Angular/NestJS work and common in advanced interviews.
theory.realWorldExample: NestJS marks a class with @Controller('users') and a method with @Get() to declare an HTTP route declaratively.

nestedTopics.title: Decorator targets
nestedTopics.explanation: class, method, accessor, property, and parameter — each with its own signature.

nestedTopics.title: Definition-time execution
nestedTopics.explanation: Decorators run once when the class is defined, before instances exist.

nestedTopics.title: Metadata
nestedTopics.explanation: Property/parameter decorators commonly record info a framework reads later.

followUps.question: Do decorators run per instance or per call?
followUps.answer: Neither — a decorator function runs once at class-definition time; any per-call behavior comes from a wrapper it installs.

followUps.question: Can a class decorator change the class?
followUps.answer: Yes — returning a new constructor replaces or extends the class; returning nothing leaves it as-is.

theory.question: How do you enable decorators, and what is the difference between legacy and TC39 standard decorators?
theory.directAnswer: Legacy (experimental) decorators require experimentalDecorators in tsconfig, optionally with emitDecoratorMetadata plus the reflect-metadata polyfill for type-based DI; they use the (target, key, descriptor) signature. The TC39 Stage-3 standard decorators, supported from TypeScript 5.0, are enabled by default, use a (value, context) signature, and emit no design metadata. They are not directly interchangeable, and frameworks like Angular and NestJS are migrating gradually.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two distinct decorator systems: the older experimental one and the newer ECMAScript-standard one.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Decorators long predated a finalized spec, so TypeScript shipped an experimental version; TC39 later standardized a different design.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Legacy is gated by a flag and uses descriptor-based signatures with optional metadata emission; standard decorators follow the spec's (value, context) contract and ship on by default.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the wrong mode breaks framework code; teams must know which their stack uses and that metadata-based DI depends on the legacy emit.
theory.realWorldExample: An Angular app sets experimentalDecorators and emitDecoratorMetadata, while a fresh library targeting TS 5+ may use standard decorators with no extra flags.

nestedTopics.title: Compiler flags
nestedTopics.explanation: experimentalDecorators and emitDecoratorMetadata gate the legacy mode and metadata.

nestedTopics.title: reflect-metadata
nestedTopics.explanation: A polyfill the runtime uses to read emitted design types for DI.

nestedTopics.title: Signature differences
nestedTopics.explanation: Legacy (target, key, descriptor) vs standard (value, context).

followUps.question: Why do TC39 decorators not support emitDecoratorMetadata?
followUps.answer: Design-metadata emission was a TypeScript-specific extension of the legacy system; the standard didn't adopt it, so type-based DI relying on it stays on legacy or uses an alternative.

scenario.question: Your NestJS service injects a repository by type, but at runtime the dependency is undefined and the app crashes. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: This is almost always a metadata setup problem. Confirm tsconfig has experimentalDecorators and emitDecoratorMetadata enabled, and that reflect-metadata is imported once at the app entry point before anything decorated loads. Without emitted design:paramtypes and the polyfill, the DI container can't see the constructor's parameter types, so it resolves the dependency to undefined. Enabling both flags and the import restores type-based injection.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A failure of metadata-driven dependency injection caused by missing compiler flags or polyfill.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Type-based DI reads design:paramtypes, which only exists when emitDecoratorMetadata is on and reflect-metadata is loaded.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: With the flags set, the compiler emits constructor param types; the container reads them via Reflect to instantiate and inject the right dependencies.

scenario.whyImportant: This is a frequent real-world setup bug; diagnosing it shows understanding of the metadata mechanism rather than treating decorators as magic.

nestedTopics.title: design:paramtypes
nestedTopics.explanation: The emitted metadata key the container reads for constructor parameter types.

nestedTopics.title: Import ordering
nestedTopics.explanation: reflect-metadata must be imported before any decorated class is evaluated.

followUps.question: What if a parameter type is an interface?
followUps.answer: Interfaces are erased, so there's no runtime type to inject; use an injection token (@Inject(TOKEN)) instead of relying on the type.

coding.question: Write a legacy method decorator @measure that logs how long the decorated method takes, preserving its return value and arguments.
coding.thoughtProcess: A legacy method decorator receives (target, propertyKey, descriptor). I save descriptor.value (the original method), then replace it with a wrapper that records the start time, calls the original via apply with this and the args, measures the elapsed time, logs it, and returns the original result. Preserving this and the return value is essential so behavior is unchanged apart from the logging.
coding.lineByLine: measure captures descriptor.value as original. It overwrites descriptor.value with a function that times the call: records start, invokes original.apply(this, args) so this and arguments are preserved, logs the elapsed milliseconds with the method name, and returns the original result unchanged. Applied with @measure, build is transparently wrapped. (Requires experimentalDecorators to compile.)
coding.timeComplexity: The decorator adds O(1) overhead per call; build itself is O(rows).

alternativeApproaches.title: TC39 standard form
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Under standard decorators the signature is (value, context); the method is the first arg and you return a replacement function rather than mutating a descriptor.
alternativeApproaches.code: function measure(value: any, _ctx: ClassMethodDecoratorContext) { return function (this: any, ...a: any[]) { const s = Date.now(); const r = value.apply(this, a); console.log(Date.now() - s); return r; }; }

followUps.question: Why use apply(this, args) instead of calling original directly?
followUps.answer: To preserve the correct this binding and forward all arguments, so the wrapped method behaves identically to the original.

systemDesign.question: Design a decorator-based cross-cutting concerns layer (logging, auth, validation, caching) for a NestJS-style service application. How do decorators fit, and what are the trade-offs at scale?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Model each concern as a decorator: method decorators for logging/timing/caching that wrap the handler, parameter decorators plus metadata for request binding and validation, and class decorators (or guards) for auth applied per controller. A DI container reads decorator-emitted metadata to wire dependencies. This keeps business logic clean and concerns reusable. The trade-offs are indirection (behavior lives outside the visible method body, hurting debuggability), a hard dependency on the experimental decorators flag and reflect-metadata, evaluation-order subtleties when stacking decorators, and the risk of hidden runtime cost in per-call wrappers. At scale you standardize a small decorator set, document execution order, and keep wrappers cheap.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An architecture where cross-cutting behavior is expressed as composable decorators rather than inline code in each method.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Concerns like auth, logging, and validation recur across every endpoint; centralizing them as decorators removes duplication and keeps handlers focused on domain logic.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Decorators run at definition time to register metadata or install wrappers; the framework/DI container reads metadata to bind requests and resolve dependencies, and stacked decorators compose around the original method.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Cross-cutting concerns are a major source of duplication and inconsistency in large services; a clean decorator layer is the standard solution but introduces real operational trade-offs interviewers want you to reason about.

nestedTopics.title: Composition and order
nestedTopics.explanation: Stacked decorators apply bottom-up (closest to the method first); order changes behavior for guards/validators, so it must be defined and documented.

nestedTopics.title: Metadata + DI
nestedTopics.explanation: emitDecoratorMetadata and reflect-metadata let the container resolve dependencies and bind parameters by type/token.

nestedTopics.title: Debuggability vs reuse
nestedTopics.explanation: Decorators hide behavior from the method body; trace logs and clear naming offset the loss of locality.

nestedTopics.title: Runtime cost
nestedTopics.explanation: Per-call wrappers (validation, caching) add overhead; keep them lean and measure hot paths.

followUps.question: How do you control the order auth, validation, and logging run in?
followUps.answer: Decorator application is bottom-up relative to the method, and frameworks define a guard/pipe/interceptor pipeline order; you rely on that documented pipeline rather than implicit decorator stacking for predictable behavior.

followUps.question: What's the migration risk to TC39 standard decorators?
followUps.answer: Signatures and metadata emission differ, so framework code and any custom metadata-based DI must be ported; you'd stage the migration and keep legacy mode until the framework fully supports the standard.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Decorators define the framework layer: Angular components/services, NestJS controllers/providers, ORM entities, and validation schemas. They register classes and bind cross-cutting concerns declaratively, with a DI container reading emitted metadata to wire everything together.
productionDeepDive.performance: Decorators evaluate once at class-definition time, so static cost is low. emitDecoratorMetadata plus reflect-metadata add bundle size and a small startup cost, and method-wrapping decorators (validation, caching, logging) add per-call overhead proportional to their work — keep hot-path wrappers lean.
productionDeepDive.security: Auth and validation decorators centralize enforcement, but order matters: a misordered guard can let unvalidated input through. Decorators relying on erased type metadata can silently fail (undefined injection); never assume a decorator ran without verifying the pipeline.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Standardize a small, documented set of decorators for common concerns so the codebase stays consistent as it grows. Avoid bespoke per-feature decorators that fragment behavior and complicate reasoning about execution order.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Decorators trade locality for reuse — behavior lives outside the method body, which hurts debuggability. Mitigate with clear naming, documentation of execution order, and tracing. Pin the decorator mode (legacy vs standard) consistently across the project.
productionDeepDive.observability: Logging/timing decorators are a natural place to emit metrics and traces uniformly across handlers. In CI, tsc plus the correct decorator/metadata flags catch misconfiguration; runtime DI errors (undefined dependencies) signal missing reflect-metadata setup.

caseStudies.problem: Needed declarative, reusable wiring for components, routes, DI, and validation without repeating boilerplate in every class.
caseStudies.solution: Decorator-driven architecture (@Component, @Controller, @Injectable, @Get, @Body) backed by emitDecoratorMetadata and reflect-metadata for type-based DI.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Concise and consistent, but adds indirection, a flag/polyfill dependency, and an eventual migration path to TC39 standard decorators.
caseStudies.lessons: Decorators excel at cross-cutting concerns when standardized and documented; over-customization and ignoring execution order create subtle, hard-to-debug failures.

keyTakeaways: Decorators are @-prefixed functions that run at class-definition time to observe, modify, annotate, or replace classes, methods, accessors, properties, and parameters.
Class and method/accessor decorators can replace their target; property and parameter decorators typically record metadata (e.g. for dependency injection).
Legacy decorators need experimentalDecorators (and emitDecoratorMetadata + reflect-metadata for type-based DI) and use the (target, key, descriptor) signature.
TC39 Stage-3 standard decorators (TS 5.0+) use a (value, context) signature, are on by default, and emit no design metadata — not interchangeable with legacy.
They power Angular, NestJS, TypeORM, and class-validator, centralizing cross-cutting concerns at the cost of added indirection and a metadata/flag dependency.
